reader.title: Lynching of "Bushy" Clark and "Frenchy" Bardeau
bases: Two men accused of horse theft and robbery were taken from guard and hanged by a committee described as a vigilance committee (A3, A4), and the wire called it a lynching (A1).

Both men were hanged without trial by a self-appointed 'committee' headlined as a 'vigilance committee' that took them from guard after it agreed 'desperate means had to be taken with desperate men' (A4); the size is not given but a committee acting together implies several men, and the stated pretext was the Lamy robbery and horse theft (A1, A3, A4).
Two separate specials from Socorro (A3, A4) and the Denver Republican wire (A1) agree that two accused Lamy robbers were hanged at Socorro on the night of Oct. 6-7.

summary.text: The lynching of "Bushy" Clark and "Frenchy" Bardeau was the hanging of two men accused of robbery and horse theft by a committee at Socorro, New Mexico Territory, on the night of October 6-7, 1881.
Taken from the guard that held them after their arrest, the two were found the next morning hanging together from a cottonwood tree with a placard reading "The fate of footpads and horse thieves."
A Denver wire dispatch carried the news to papers from California to Virginia, and none of the reports gave the race of either man.
About ten days before the hanging, four men had robbed the store of Browne & Manzanares at Lamy in daylight and ridden off on horses belonging to the firm, according to dispatches from Socorro.

The Denver wire described the two men later lynched as former members of "the notorious Stockton gang," and the Chicago Tribune's correspondent called Clark an old offender from the Allison and Stockton horse thieves of Durango, Colorado.
Of Bardeau, the correspondent wrote only that he was a bad man.

Three heavily armed men rode into Socorro and were watched until one of their horses was identified as stolen from Lamy, the Tribune correspondent wrote; officers then arrested two of them after a chase, and the third escaped.
The Las Vegas Daily Gazette's Socorro dispatch dated the arrest to Wednesday evening, while the Tribune account placed it on Thursday, less than twenty-four hours before the bodies were found.
According to the Tribune, the prisoners carried stolen revolvers and knives, "openly confessed the robbery," and were put under guard and heavily chained.
The same account said a committee "quietly agreed" that "desperate means had to be taken with desperate men," warned the prisoners, and called a priest before taking them out.
Both men were hanged together, "chained arm to arm and foot to foot," from a cottonwood that the Gazette placed on Methodist avenue and the Tribune near a spot called Death Alley.

The Tribune correspondent wrote that they died by strangulation and that the bodies were left hanging for several hours so that all who wished could see them and read the placard pinned to their backs.
The wire said the lynching took place "last night," and both Socorro dispatches said the bodies were discovered on the morning of Friday, October 7.
No report of an inquest, of arrests of the lynchers, or of any official inquiry appears in the coverage.
Weekly news summaries repeated the story into late October, the Grant County Herald of Wisconsin reporting that the two were lynched "near Socorro" for horse-stealing.

The first reports came from a Denver Republican special dated October 7, which named the victims only as Clark, alias "Butch," and "Frenchy" and appeared the next day in the Cheyenne Daily Leader and the Sacramento Daily Record-Union.

Over the following days the dispatch ran under headlines such as "Judge Lynch" in the Los Angeles Herald, "Lynch Law in New Mexico" in the Arizona Weekly Citizen and "Desperadoes Lynched" in the Dallas Herald.
It also appeared in the Richmond Daily Dispatch, the Savannah Morning News and the Austin Weekly Democratic Statesman.
Copying garbled the details, so that Clark's alias appeared as "Butch," "Butcher" and "Beach," and the robbed town as Lamy, "Laramie" and "Saney."

The Socorro specials treated the hanging with approval and humor: the Gazette headlined that the thieves were treated to a "Tight Rope Entertainment" and concluded that the placard showed "Socorro is a bad place for bad men."

The Chicago Tribune ran its correspondent's letter under the heading "A Neck-Tie Sociable," described the prisoners as a "walking arsenal," and wrote that after the priest's visit "the necktie social began."
By the time the item reached a Kentucky news digest on October 18, it read only that "L. Nordean and 'Bushy' Clark, horsethieves, were lynched at Lama."
The second victim's name varied: the Tribune printed "Bardeau," the Grant County Herald "Bardean" and the South Kentuckian "L. Nordean," while the wire gave only "Frenchy."
The Kentucky digest also placed the lynching at "Lama," a name close to Lamy, where the robbery occurred, but every dispatch from New Mexico placed the hanging in Socorro.

accounts.label: Denver Republican wire
accounts.gist: Two robbers of the Stockton gang, Clark alias "Butch" and "Frenchy", were lynched last night at Socorro; a week earlier they robbed a commission house at Lamy.

accounts.label: Las Vegas Gazette's Socorro special
accounts.gist: Two of four Lamy store robbers were arrested Wednesday evening and found this morning hanging from a cottonwood on Methodist avenue with a placard.

accounts.label: Chicago Tribune's Socorro correspondent
accounts.gist: Officers arrested two of three armed men after a chase; they confessed; a committee agreed on 'desperate means', called a priest and hanged them chained together near Death Alley, leaving them up for hours with a placard.

framing.detail: The Las Vegas Gazette headlined that the thieves 'Were Treated to a Tight Rope Enter tainment' and said the placard showed 'Socorro is a bad place for bad men'.
The Chicago Tribune headlined 'A NECK-TIE SOCIABLE', called the victims desperadoes and a 'walking arsenal', and described the hanging as a 'necktie social'.
Papers from Wyoming to Virginia ran the Denver wire under headlines such as 'Exit "Butch" and "Frenchy."', 'Judge Lynch', 'Lynch Law in New Mexico' and 'Desperadoes Lynched'.
News digests reduced it to one line naming the men as horsethieves.

conflicts.note: Bardeau comes from the Socorro correspondent (A4); 'L. Nordean' in a late Kentucky digest looks like a garble of it.
Variants arise in telegraphic copying of the Denver wire.
The New Mexico dispatches place the hanging in Socorro itself; Lamy was the site of the robbery, and 'Lama' appears only in the Kentucky digest.
